British American Tobacco expects mid-teens New Category revenue growth in 2026, making execution against that target particularly important. Management also aims to reduce net leverage to between 2 and 2.5 times adjusted EBITDA by year-end. Stronger smokeless product margins and continued debt reduction could reinforce JPMorgan's bullish outlook. The investment case ultimately depends on maintaining strong cash returns while successfully transitioning beyond traditional tobacco. title: Google's latest TPUs show Broadcom remains central: JPM - TradingView
content: On Monday, Google GOOGGOOGL revealed its latest pair of tensor processing unit systems, and the analysts at J.P. Morgan find that Broadcom AVGO remains a key partner in the development process. Broadcome shares edged up 2.5% by afternoon trading on Tuesday. "The new inferencing TPU SKU is dubbed the v8i Max and is designed for massive context windows (built to handle much larger AI workloads in the same rack space)," said J.P. Morgan analyst Harlan Sur in an investor note. "Based on the architectural details provided by GOOGL, we believe the v8i Max is highly consistent with the 3nm Broadcom TPU program we highlighted in our Fall Series Presentation, as the v8i Max has four TPU compute chips in a single package (delivering double the compute with the same physical footprint) versus the current-generation v8i, which has two compute chips in a single package." The details prompted J.P. Morgan to reiterate its Overweight rating on Broadcom. The TPU 8tx was designed for secure and confidential inference and small-scale training for regulated enterprises and governments. Meanwhile, the TPU 8i Max, which takes two low-latency TPU 8i chips and combines them into a single package, was developed to address the memory bottleneck that can occur when dozens of AI agents are working together across a software codebase. "Based on our checks, we believe the v8i Max is set to ramp in ~2H27, while the more important next-generation 2nm TPU SKU (v9.5 / v10) remains on track for production in mid-2028 (2nm, 8 compute dies, 8 SRAM dies, 16 HBM stacks, 400G SERDES I/O)," Sur added. J.P. Morgan concluded that Broadcom remains central to Google's highest-performing TPUs, which should continue to benefit revenue through at least calendar year 2031.DisclaimerContent provided by Seeking Alpha is intended for information purposes only, and that Seeking Alpha does not offer any personalist investment advice and is not a licensed securities dealer, broker, US investment adviser or investment bank. title: A brighter productivity outlook for the AI era - J.P. Morgan Private Bank
content:
The Private Bank’s mission is to build, preserve & transform our client’s wealth. We work with a variety of clients to help them achieve their unique ambitions. Our world-class economists, strategists, and investment specialists share their timely ideas and perspectives. We have worked with clients for more than 200 years to help them achieve their unique ambitions. AI’s promise is becoming real. As the technology races forward, trillions of dollars are flowing into semiconductors, data centers and power suppliers – the new AI ecosystem. But will AI make the economy more productive and, if so, by how much, how quickly and for whom? No force has a greater impact on our Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions (LTCMAs) than productivity growth, the pace at which an economy turns its labor and capital into more output. Productivity underpins economic growth, living standards, corporate earnings, inflation and interest rates. As the economist Paul Krugman once said, “Productivity isn’t everything, but in the long run, it is almost everything.” We believe AI will raise productivity meaningfully and durably over our 10- to 15-year horizon, reshaping the nature of work and patterns of investment. While we have incrementally incorporated AI’s potential into our LTCMAs since 2023, the dramatic acceleration in capabilities and investment now requires more sophisticated analysis. To capture that shift, we have rebuilt our AI methodology and embedded it within our macroeconomic building blocks. Anchored around a Cobb-Douglas production function, it attributes an economy’s output to its labor and capital, and how efficiently those are used (see Methodology Handbook). In that framework, AI lifts labor productivity, measured as output per hour worked, through two channels. First, it makes existing work more efficient, enabling the same people and machines to produce more (total factor productivity, or TFP). Second, it equips workers with improved tools, systems and infrastructure as investment scales (capital deepening).[1] Here, we present our new methodology and the insight it delivers. Source: Tyna Eloundou, Sam Manning, Pamela Mishkin et al., “GPTs are GPTs: Labor Market Impact Potential of LLMs,” Science, June 2024; J.P. Morgan Asset
Management. *Exposure is defined as AI reducing the time to complete a task by at least 50% at equivalent quality. **LLMs (large language models) are AI
systems trained on text and code, used directly as a chatbot. AI software refers to the specialized tools built on top of these systems, such as documentation
search, code execution and image generation. The frontier combines tasks reachable by AI software (roughly 66%, following Eloundou et al.), with an additional
layer of robotics deemed commercially viable by 2040, including autonomous trucking, warehouse and factory automation, construction and agriculture,
bringing the total to 72%. Tasks requiring a general-purpose humanoid robot are excluded. Occupations reflect major U.S. groups, weighted by each
occupation’s share of total U.S. wages. What might lie ahead? Forecasting productivity is difficult even in ordinary times, and profound technological change makes the challenge even greater. Our updated methodology should offer a solid framework from which to reason and refine as new evidence develops. For total factor productivity, we focus on the specific tasks AI can perform, and how efficiently. We then map those gains across the economy, an approach grounded in Hulten’s theorem as applied by Daron Acemoglu and others.[6] We estimate capital deepening by projecting how AI-related investment affects the economy’s productive capital stock, net of depreciation and “crowding out” (displacing other productive investments). By 2040, we believe, AI adoption will have shifted to more embedded agentic,[7] and even robotic, workflows, spreading beyond knowledge-intensive early users to routine work across sectors. But diffusion will be gradual. We expect a slow start, with adoption accelerating in the early 2030s and then tapering as remaining use cases become harder or less economically attractive. Scaling AI will require integrating with legacy systems and redesigning operating models. Friction may be most acute where oversight and liability management require human involvement, particularly where AI missteps could prove costly. This gradual pace is an important premise of our macroeconomic and asset class assumptions. Steady uptake should limit rapid, economy-wide job displacement and keep broad inflation contained, even as the build-out strains supply chains in the near term. In our base case, AI boosts U.S. TFP growth above its pre-AI trend by roughly 40bps, to 1.2% annually,[8] and it lifts U.S. capital stock growth by about 30bps, to 2.3% per year. Together, this raises our total U.S. labor productivity forecast by 50bps vs. our pre-AI baseline, to 2.2%. Small gains compound: A sustained 50bps boost over 15 years would make the U.S. economy 7%–8% larger than it otherwise would have been. Given this is our fourth year incorporating AI into our assumptions, this year’s incremental productivity lift vs. last year is 20bps. Relative to other forecasts, our view appears cautiously optimistic. The 40bps AI-driven TFP uplift exceeds the Congressional Budget Office’s more conservative 10bps estimate while landing in the lower half of the OECD’s 27bps to 85bps scenario range.[9] Against that backdrop, our analysis first builds a baseline forecast for the U.S., then extends it globally, accounting for regional variation. Beyond TFP, our outlook hinges on how much the surge in AI spending ultimately increases productivity. Since 2023, AI demand and enthusiasm have driven U.S. hyperscalers to cumulatively invest close to USD 1.6 trillion in capex, spanning data centers, power, semiconductors and networking. Globally, the total exceeds USD 2 trillion over the same period.[13] Our outlook for capital deepening builds on four factors: the path of AI spending, its composition, the rate of depreciation and the extent to which it crowds out other productive capex. Broadly, the first two variables are additive to growth, while the latter two detract. Developed markets appear better positioned to deploy AI at scale, given their large service sectors, strong digital infrastructure and supportive institutions. Where workforces are shrinking – from Japan and China to the U.S., Germany and Italy – firms will have a greater incentive to use AI to help offset demographic challenges. But economic gains will vary between AI enablers, which supply key inputs for the build-out, and adopters, which successfully integrate AI (Exhibit 2). The two can be mutually reinforcing: Better tools and infrastructure can speed up adoption, and durable monetization can incentivize further investment. Source: Eloundou et al. (2024), International Monetary Fund, J.P. Morgan Asset Management. The IMF AI Preparedness Index scores countries’ AI adoption
readiness across digital infrastructure, human capital, innovation and regulation (0 to 1, rescaled to 0 to 100). Task exposure is the estimated share of work
tasks AI could perform based on each country’s occupation mix, building on the approach of Eloundou et al. with an added robotics layer. The U.S. leads as both an enabler and an adopter, registering the largest AI-driven TFP boost in our forecast universe. Its concentration of frontier model developers, hyperscalers and software platforms is unmatched. Corporate America also has the financial strength and appetite to sustain the AI build-out, supported by a flexible, innovation-oriented business environment. Meanwhile, Europe’s early AI gains skew toward a few key enablers in areas where it has outsize global influence, notably semiconductor manufacturing equipment and power grid and infrastructure. Broader gains should follow as AI diffuses across Europe’s services-heavy economies (several of which are more AI-exposed than the U.S.). However, its fragmentated single market, legal and regulatory burdens, labor constraints and energy supply vulnerabilities may slow AI’s rollout. China is building a parallel AI ecosystem, with homegrown models, domestic chip production and a push into robotics. China’s cost competitiveness may prove an advantage, while deployment of AI (which is often state-mandated) across industrial and consumer sectors could drive economy-level productivity gains. Chinese models are also gaining traction globally, recently overtaking U.S. models in token usage on OpenRouter, a widely used developer gateway. Still, weaker monetization by Chinese firms and export controls on advanced U.S. chips should restrain investment and development. Taiwan and South Korea should continue to benefit from their central role in global tech supply chains, notably in advanced semiconductor manufacturing. Both economies rank among the largest upward revisions to our GDP growth assumptions. That competitive position is a strength but also a risk, as economic nationalism and geopolitical uncertainty drive the U.S. and China toward onshore alternatives. Finally, Japan arguably has the strongest incentive to adopt AI, given its aging workforce, but long-tenure norms may hinder diffusion. Our base case is just one plausible path among many alternate scenarios (Exhibits 3A and 3B). AI could disappoint if regulation or social backlash restrains adoption, or if capex resets more sharply due to obsolescence, margin pressure, tighter financing or power constraints. Even with broad diffusion, AI may still underdeliver if oversight adds more work, time savings shift to leisure rather than new tasks, or skill gaps and worker preferences become binding constraints. Such a downside scenario could see AI reach only a quarter of tasks by 2040 (vs. 40% in our base case) and annual TFP growth settle below 1%. Source: J.P. Total factor productivity is for the private nonfarm business sector, 10-year trailing average of annual growth rates. The capex outlook anchors to reported and projected capex from the top five U.S. hyperscalers, with additional assumptions for neocloud, enterprise and government AI infrastructure. Despite the profound impact AI has already had on markets, we don’t think its potential is fully appreciated. Investors will seek to identify where value accrues, whether through profit growth, risk premia or pricing power. We believe portfolios can best capture that potential by balancing exposure across the AI value chain and funding cycle, spanning public and private markets. That calls for strategic discipline and tactical flexibility. Returns have so far favored the AI enablers. But the set of beneficiaries already extends beyond hyperscalers and semiconductors into infrastructure and power. As adoption spreads, more sectors should participate. This expectation underpins our view that equities will deliver stronger, broader earnings growth and sustain structurally higher margins and valuations than they would have in a world without AI. Value should shift toward adopters deploying AI, in areas such as predictive analytics, speed to market, product fit and supply chain management. Financial services, health care, retail and logistics firms are among such early adopters and tend to rank higher in measures of AI exposure and labor intensity (Exhibit 4). The U.S. remains at the core of global allocations, offering exposure to a vibrant culture of innovation, tech-heavy indices and deep capital markets. It ranks among the highest in profit margins in our forecast universe. In Europe, value stands to remain concentrated in “pick-and-shovel” enablers until adoption broadens. And while Asian companies should remain essential to tech supply chains, the strength of the current capex wave may have pulled forward some revenue and margin gains, making stock selection crucial after recent investor optimism. We anticipate that the capex build-out will contribute to our outlook for higher real rates, elevated term premia and steeper yield curves, even if AI produces disinflationary effects over time. Credit issuance is rising as hyperscalers become a more pronounced presence in debt markets, lifting index quality despite biasing spreads wider. Investors may find relative value in issuers that can fund investment without stretching balance sheets, though complex financing structures and off-balance sheet obligations warrant scrutiny. Commodities supply key inputs. Infrastructure and real estate add critical capacity across power, cooling, transmission and storage, and offer inflation resilience via contracted cash flows. But risk profiles vary widely, from regulated grid power to data centers and on-site generation, and warrant specialized underwriting. Private equity managers can enhance value creation and improve operating efficiency by deploying AI across portfolio companies. Meanwhile, venture capital backs many of the AI-native companies now growing to unprecedented scale in private markets, albeit with highly skewed outcomes. Private credit in turn finances parts of the AI build-out, though deal terms will need to evolve in tandem, given direct lending’s meaningful exposure to software and technology. And as disruption accelerates, hedge funds may capitalize on dislocations. Above all, manager selection will be critical, as outcomes may vary considerably by exposure, vintage and strategy. As we model the world in 2040, we believe the AI ecosystem will evolve in ways that prove transformative. This should drive efficiency gains, support margin resilience and unlock new growth opportunities that extend well beyond the tech sector. But the path of adoption and diffusion won’t be smooth, bringing higher volatility and wider dispersion that necessitate a disciplined, diversified approach. Investors should build AI exposure intentionally and prepare to shift course as a new era of innovation and value creation unfolds. A bank group led by JPMorgan Chase (NYSE:JPM | JPM Price Prediction) may offer one of the year’s largest discounts to clear buyout debt it got stuck holding. After the close on November 9, 2026, people familiar with the matter said bankers scheduled investor meetings to discuss selling nearly $2 billion of Qualtrics International debt in the high-yield bond market. Initial talk points to a coupon of at least 8% and a price of about 85 cents on the dollar. Nothing has been launched or priced, and JPMorgan has issued no filing or press release on the sale. JPMorgan closed at $342.08 that day, up 2.28%, before the report came out. The stock was $342.11 late in after-hours trading, which shows no meaningful reaction. For shareholders, the question is whether a loss on one stuck buyout matters. JPMorgan carries a $908.51 billion market value. The debt financed Qualtrics’ $6.75 billion purchase of Press Ganey Forsta. Qualtrics is private and owned by Silver Lake and, reportedly, the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board, so it has no public financials to check. In March, the plan was a $5.3 billion package: a $3.3 billion leveraged loan and $2 billion of high-yield bonds. On March 17, the banks stopped it after investors objected to Qualtrics’ exposure to the software selloff and fears of AI disruption. By May 6, the group expected paper losses of more than $500 million and prepared to fund the deal itself. That made it the year’s biggest hung deal. Banks promised to provide the debt but could not sell it, so it sits on their own books and ties up capital. A reported 11 institutions, including Goldman Sachs (NYSE:GS), Morgan Stanley (NYSE:MS) and UBS (NYSE:UBS), provided bridge financing. On October 15, JPMorgan considered splitting the debt into about $2 billion each of bonds and loans, and the plan for the loan portion remains undisclosed. A coupon is the fixed interest a bond pays on its face value, and selling at a discount means buyers pay less than face value, so the seller takes the gap. At the indicated price, the bonds would raise about $1.7 billion. Current yield, the annual coupon divided by the price paid, would be about 9.4%, although the final size, price, coupon, and maturity are not set. The loss estimate covers the whole bank group, and JPMorgan’s share has never been disclosed. For scale, its Commercial & Investment Bank earned $8.2 billion of net income in the third quarter alone. Selling cheaply still makes sense because it locks in a known loss and frees the balance sheet for fee-paying deals. The price shows how investors now value software buyouts when AI threatens subscription revenue, and if that pressure keeps building, bond buyers could find the extra yield too thin. Jamie Dimon, chairman and CEO at the time of the October 13, 2026 earnings call, already sounded cautious: “We are tightening up credit a little bit. I think some of the credit terms have gotten a little bit loose.” A clean sale would tell private-equity sponsors that stuck debt can clear at a price. A weak reception would make banks slower to commit to the next software buyout. This loss is likely small next to JPMorgan’s earnings power, and clearing it would remove a drag on underwriting capacity. The stock trades at 14 times trailing earnings and 13 times forward earnings, below an analyst target of $373.48. Its 52-week range runs from $275.06 to $364.68. title: J.P. Morgan AM forecasts European ETF assets will exceed $6tn by 2030 - Funds Global MENA
content: Firm expects retail platforms, retirement reform and the move of active ETFs into core portfolios will drive another rapid expansion of the European market. J.P. Morgan Asset Management expects European exchange-traded fund assets to rise to “well north of $6tn” by the end of 2030, supported by retail adoption, pension reform and greater institutional use of active products. Travis Spence, global head of ETFs at New York-based J.P. Morgan Asset Management, says the European industry is on course for a second consecutive record year across assets, flows, trading volumes and issuance. The market had broadly doubled every five years, he adds, and expects the global ETF industry  will exceed $35tn by 2030. Retail participation could grow more quickly than the wider European market, driven by digital investment platforms and changes to retirement systems, particularly in Germany. Spence describes the opportunity as a “saver-to-investor movement”, arguing that ETFs’ cost and ease of use make them a natural vehicle for bringing younger and first-time investors into capital markets. Institutional demand is also changing. Pension funds, insurers and sovereign investors are increasingly moving active ETFs into core allocations rather than using them only for limited portfolio purposes, he says. Active ETFs will be a major part of the expansion. J.P. Morgan AM forecasts that global active ETF assets will increase from about $2.5tn today to more than $7tn by 2030. The US now has more active than passive ETFs by number, a reversal that Spence says had occurred within the past two years “You now have a two-and-a-half-trillion-dollar industry that didn’t exist five years ago,” he says. Its increased scale and breadth means that “any large investor has to take notice” of the products now available. J.P. Morgan AM has 177 ETFs globally, of which 127 are active. Its European Ucits range comprises 58 exchange-traded products of which 46 are active ETFs. The US giant began developing active Ucits ETFs in 2018 and has continued to broaden the range. Rather than building separate investment operations, the firm uses the same portfolio managers, research analysts and investment processes for ETFs, mutual funds and separate accounts. “Our portfolio managers do both,” Spence says, adding that the company wants clients to choose the vehicle most appropriate for them. He rejects the suggestion that the rise of ETFs necessarily amounts to cannibalisation of mutual funds. Although the broader industry has experienced mutual fund outflows and ETF inflows, J.P. Morgan had recorded growth across both its mutual funds and ETFs. “We don’t necessarily see that it is a cannibalisation,” he says. “There’s an adjustment happening within the industry.” Product innovation should provide a further source of growth. Spence highlights derivative-based ETFs that package income generation or lower-volatility equity exposure into a single trade. J.P. Morgan’s derivative-income ETF suite has gathered over $90bn across its Ucits and US platforms, while the global category has grown to roughly $170bn since emerging in 2020. Spence says European investors have demonstrated “insatiable demand for income”. Fixed income is another large opportunity, particularly for active ETFs. The wrapper allows investors to obtain a diversified bond portfolio through a security trading like an equity, avoiding some of the cost and complexity of purchasing individual bonds. J.P. Morgan has also begun tokenising money market funds and expects tokenisation to become “a much bigger area” over the next five years, although Spence says that the pace of investor adoption remains uncertain. The firm is separately applying artificial intelligence to its Spectrum portfolio-management system, using the technology to analyse more than 40 years of proprietary investment data to help portfolio managers assess markets from multiple perspectives. title: JPM Expects M&A Slowdown in 2027: Can Private Equity Exits Offset? - The Globe and Mail
content: JPMorgan JPM expects global mergers and acquisitions (M&A) activity to moderate in 2027 following a robust performance earlier this year. In a Nov. 6 interview with Fortune, Charlie Bouckaert, the bank's global head of M&A, indicated that fewer large transactions could materialize next year, although bigger deals are likely to continue dominating activity.The slowdown is likely to challenge JPMorgan's investment banking (IB) fee growth. In third-quarter 2026, IB fees increased 14% year over year to $3 billion, driven by a 32% jump in advisory fees to $1.2 billion. Reduced deal volumes could make sustaining this momentum difficult.Despite the softer M&A outlook, increasing pressure on private equity firms to monetize investments could create opportunities. Bouckaert expects exits to accelerate in the second half of 2027 as aging portfolios, approaching refinancing deadlines and investor liquidity demands prompt sponsors to pursue transactions.Per PitchBook data cited by Fortune, private equity firms held 33,853 unsold investments as of Sept. 30, 2026, indicating a substantial backlog of potential transactions. Moreover, sponsors could increasingly explore continuation funds and secondary transactions instead of outright asset sales. These alternatives may generate incremental advisory and financing mandates for JPMorgan.While moderating M&A activity could temper JPMorgan's advisory revenue growth in 2027, rising private equity exits and alternative liquidity transactions may provide some offset. The bank's established IB franchise positions it to capture these opportunities. However, the timing and execution of sponsor exits, alongside uncertain transaction volumes, will determine whether incremental fees can meaningfully cushion the slowdown. Two close peers of JPMorgan are Goldman SachsGS and Morgan StanleyMS.For Goldman, slower M&A activity in 2027 could constrain advisory fee growth. However, rising private equity exits, continuation funds and secondary transactions may create fresh revenue opportunities. Goldman's strong dealmaking franchise and sponsor relationships position it to benefit, potentially cushioning the impact of weaker overall transaction volumes.For Morgan Stanley, a slowdown in M&A activity in 2027 could weigh on advisory fee growth. However, rising private equity exits and increasing adoption of continuation funds and secondary transactions could create new advisory opportunities. Morgan Stanley’s strong IB franchise and sponsor relationships position it to capture these mandates, partially offsetting weaker dealmaking activity. title: DTE sells non-utility DTE Vantage business to J.P Morgan - Daily Energy Insider
content: DTE Energy is selling its non-utility DTE Vantage business for approximately $3 billion to institutional investors advised by the Global Infrastructure group at J.P. Morgan Asset Management. The transaction advances DTE’s long-term strategy and continued focus on customer affordability, while strengthening its ability to make significant utility investments. To the latter point, it will support a substantial increase in investment in the electric and gas utilities, which will total approximately $44 billion over the next five years. This includes investment to serve growing data center demand. “DTE Vantage has been a strong non-utility business and valued part of DTE Energy for more than 30 years,” Joi Harris, DTE president and CEO, said. “This transaction advances our strategy to focus our resources on our regulated electric and gas utilities, where we see significant opportunities to invest on behalf of customers and communities. The sale supports our plan to deliver meaningful affordability benefits for customers, strengthens our ability to execute a substantial utility investment plan and positions DTE as a high-growth, premium utility with a stronger long-term outlook.” The sale includes the sale of primarily all DTE Vantage assets, except EES Coke. The company has invested nearly $4.1 billion in its utilities through the third quarter and remains on track to invest $6.1 billion this year. The capital investments are strengthening and modernizing the company’s electric and natural gas systems and supporting the transition to cleaner power generation. Lazard is acting as exclusive financial advisor to DTE Energy, and Kirkland & Ellis is acting as legal advisor to DTE Energy. The sale is expected to close in the first half of 2027. DTE Energy, based in Detroit, serves 2.3 million electric customers in Southeast Michigan and 1.4 million natural gas customers across Michigan. title: JP Morgan Athlete Center of Excellence: athletes need a financial playbook now more than ever - Fortune
content:
Adam Frank is head of wealth planning and advice at J.P. Morgan Wealth Management. He and his team are responsible for wealth planning, thought leadership and strategic planning for individual clients, and he oversees the firm’s Athlete Center of Excellence. J.P. Morgan’s Athlete Center of Excellence and the JPMorganChase Athlete Council are both named in this piece. For years, the playbook was simple: athletes focused on their sport first, and financial planning came later. Only after signing a professional contract did they typically hire advisors, accountants and attorneys — and start thinking seriously about managing their wealth. That timeline often no longer reflects reality. The sports industry has made tremendous strides in creating new ways for athletes to earn money. The next challenge is ensuring they have the knowledge and support to manage it. Today, many athletes start earning meaningful income long before they turn professional. The College Sports Commission estimates that student-athletes received $1.77 billion in revenue-sharing pay in 2025-2026. Name, Image and Likeness (NIL) opportunities have accelerated that shift, giving student-athletes access to sponsorships and business opportunities while they’re still in school. At the same time, the demand for financial guidance is growing. The 2022 NCAA Student-Athlete Well-Being Study found that many have a strong desire for more resources on financial literacy and taxes. There is a big focus on creating more earning opportunities for athletes. We now need to put the same energy into helping athletes prepare for the financial responsibilities that come with them. Too often, financial education starts after the money arrives. By then, habits have already formed and important decisions may have already been made. The reality is that some of the most important financial choices for athletes happen before they sign a major contract. How do taxes work? How much should I save? How do I navigate money conversations with friends and family? Who should I trust? These aren’t professional athlete questions. They’re life questions. And athletes are encountering them earlier than ever before. One thing I’ve learned from conversations with athletes in my role at J.P. Morgan’s Athlete Center of Excellence is that they’re eager for this guidance. I’ve spoken with current players who — when they were earning NIL income — budgeted for spending and invested the rest, only to find themselves short on cash when tax payments were due. They had the right pieces in place but only became fully engaged when there was a need to be. I’ve seen a lot of players learn to bring in their financial advisor this way — relying on the advisor to then quarterback communication among their agent, attorney and accountant. Athletes should not be expected to be financial experts. Just as athletes rely on coaches, trainers, nutritionists and medical professionals, they should be able to rely on trusted specialists for financial guidance. But athletes should also have basic financial knowledge so they can ask thoughtful questions, evaluate advice and make informed decisions. I often encourage athletes to think of themselves as the CEO of their own business. You don’t have to master every function of the organization, but you should understand how the pieces fit together and remain engaged in the decisions that affect your future. That mindset has become increasingly important as athletes build personal brands and create new income streams earlier in their careers. Today’s athletes aren’t just managing contracts. Many are navigating partnerships, content opportunities, business ventures and NIL deals at a young age. The financial complexity has increased, and adequate preparation needs to increase with it. The answer isn’t limiting opportunity for athletes. It’s building a stronger foundation of education and support around it. First, we need to start earlier. Financial fundamentals should be introduced in high school, before athletes encounter significant earnings. By the time money arrives, the framework for managing it should already be in place. Second, financial education cannot be a one-time conversation. Athletes’ needs evolve as they move from high school to college, turn professional and transition out of sports. The guidance they receive should evolve alongside them. One of the reasons the JPMorganChase Athlete Council was created was to hear directly from athletes. This way, we can better understand the financial questions they’re facing and develop resources that reflect their real-world experiences, not our assumptions. Athletic careers are unlike almost any other profession. Most people earn income over several decades. Athletes often earn a huge portion of their career income over a much shorter period of time. Opportunities can arrive unexpectedly, and they can disappear just as quickly. If we want athletes to thrive not only during their playing careers but throughout the rest of their lives, we need to start with financial education long before the first major paycheck arrives.
